claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Newsom et al., 2020; Bagasra and Prilliman, 2004; Gomes et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Various degrees of acquired immunity can be observed in almost all eukaryotes.
claims.source: Advances over the last two decades in comparative and evolutionary immunology have revealed complex mechanisms underlying the adaptability of immune response in prokaryotic bacteria and archaea, and various degrees of acquired immunity can be observed in almost all eukaryotes (Newsom et al., 2020; Bagasra and Prilliman, 2004; Gomes et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Newsom et al., 2020; Bagasra and Prilliman, 2004; Gomes et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Immune priming is characterized by persistent activation of the immune system following the first immune challenge, resulting in an enhanced immune response to the second challenge.
claims.source: Immune priming is characterized by the persistent activation of the immune system following the first immune challenge, resulting in an enhanced immune response to the second challenge.
claims.evidence: Defined in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Immune training and immune memory are biphasic, meaning immune response returns to baseline before the second challenge.
claims.source: In contrast, immune training and immune memory are biphasic, meaning immune response returns to baseline before the second challenge.
claims.evidence: Defined in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Immune priming and immune training are pathogen-nonspecific responses.
claims.source: While immune priming and immune training are pathogen-nonspecific responses, immune memory operates in a pathogen-specific manner, i.e., the same pathogen must be involved in both the first and second challenges (homologous infection; solid line).
claims.evidence: Defined in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Immune memory operates in a pathogen-specific manner requiring the same pathogen in both challenges.
claims.source: While immune priming and immune training are pathogen-nonspecific responses, immune memory operates in a pathogen-specific manner, i.e., the same pathogen must be involved in both the first and second challenges (homologous infection; solid line).
claims.evidence: Defined in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claims.claim: More than 150 distinct prokaryotic immune mechanisms have been identified through whole-genome sequencing and comparative analysis.
claims.source: Whole-genome sequencing and comparative analysis of hundreds of prokaryotic organisms have led to the discovery of genomic islands that accumulate immune-related genes, enabling the identification of more than 150 distinct prokaryotic immune mechanisms (Bernheim et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Bernheim et al., 2024.

claims.claim: Many prokaryotic immune mechanisms are present to some extent in eukaryotes.
claims.source: Notably, many of these mechanisms are also present to some extent in eukaryotes, indicating that particularly cell-autonomous immune mechanisms are remarkably conserved across the tree of life (Mayo-Muñoz et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Mayo-Muñoz et al., 2023.

claims.claim: Cell-autonomous immune mechanisms are remarkably conserved across the tree of life.
claims.source: Notably, many of these mechanisms are also present to some extent in eukaryotes, indicating that particularly cell-autonomous immune mechanisms are remarkably conserved across the tree of life (Mayo-Muñoz et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Mayo-Muñoz et al., 2023.

claims.claim: Immune mechanisms that evolved in prokaryotes as protection against mobile genetic elements and pathogens were later adopted and repurposed by eukaryotic immune systems.
claims.source: The prevailing hypothesis for this phenomenon is that immune mechanisms that evolved during the rapid evolution of prokaryotes, as protection against mobile genetic elements and other pathogens, were later adopted and repurposed by eukaryotic immune systems.
claims.evidence: This is presented as a prevailing hypothesis in the field.

claims.claim: Acquisition of immune traits likely occurred through horizontal gene transfer mediated by retrotransposons.
claims.source: The acquisition of these immune traits likely occurred through horizontal gene transfer mediated by retrotransposons, highlighting the central role of domesticated mobile genetic elements in the evolution of the eukaryotic immune system (Wein and Sorek, 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Wein and Sorek, 2022.

claims.claim: The CRISPR-Cas system is widely present in most archaea and many bacteria.
claims.source: This system is widely present in most archaea and many bacteria, where it serves as a defense mechanism against bacteriophages (Rath et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Rath et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The CRISPR-Cas system serves as a defense mechanism against bacteriophages in prokaryotes.
claims.source: This system is widely present in most archaea and many bacteria, where it serves as a defense mechanism against bacteriophages (Rath et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Rath et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Bacteria and archaea can recognize foreign nucleic acids, cleave them into smaller fragments, and integrate these fragments into their own genome during bacteriophage infection.
claims.source: When a bacterium or archaeon is infected by a bacteriophage, it can recognize the foreign nucleic acids, cleave them into smaller fragments, and integrate these fragments into its own genome.
claims.evidence: This describes the established mechanism of CRISPR-Cas systems.

claims.claim: Viral DNA fragments are inserted into a specific region of the host genome known as CRISPR, which acts as a repository of previous viral encounters.
claims.source: Viral DNA fragments are inserted into a specific region of the host genome known as CRISPR, which acts as a repository of previous viral encounters (Wang et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Upon subsequent viral infection, the CRISPR locus is transcribed, producing CRISPR-pre-mRNA, which is then cleaved into individual CRISPR RNAs.
claims.source: Upon subsequent viral infection, the CRISPR locus is transcribed, producing CRISPR-pre-mRNA, which is then cleaved into individual CRISPR RNAs.
claims.evidence: This describes the established mechanism of CRISPR-Cas systems.

claims.claim: Short RNA fragments from CRISPR guide Cas nucleases to perform sequence-specific cleavage of viral genetic material.
claims.source: These short RNA fragments guide Cas nucleases to perform sequence-specific cleavage of viral genetic material (Hille et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Hille et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The CRISPR-Cas system is regarded as a clear example of adaptive immunity in prokaryotes.
claims.source: This sophisticated mechanism is widely regarded as a clear example of adaptive immunity since the integration of viral sequences into the host genome serves as a form of immune memory, while sequence-specific cleavage ensures the specificity of the immune response (Jiang and Doudna, 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Jiang and Doudna, 2017.

claims.claim: Key enzymes that protect prokaryotes from mobile genetic elements are co-opted transposases derived from retrotransposons.
claims.source: Interestingly, key enzymes that protect prokaryotes from mobile genetic elements are co-opted transposases derived from retrotransposons (Koonin and Krupovic, 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Koonin and Krupovic, 2015.

claims.claim: Enzymes responsible for somatic recombination (Rag1 and Rag2) in T and B lymphocytes are derived from the Transib family of retrotransposons.
claims.source: A similar phenomenon is observed in the adaptive immune system of jawed vertebrates, where the enzymes responsible for somatic recombination (Rag1 and Rag2) in T and B lymphocytes are derived from the Transib family of retrotransposons (Huang et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Huang et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Endogenous transposons Ty1 and Ty3 play a central role in acquiring copies of viral nucleic acids and integrating them into the insect genome.
claims.source: Another example, which will be discussed in detail later in this review, is the adaptive antiviral immunity in insects. In this system, endogenous transposons Ty1 and Ty3 play a central role in acquiring copies of viral nucleic acids and integrating them into the genome, thus creating a long-lasting and heritable immune memory (Saleh et al., 2009; Tassetto et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Saleh et al., 2009; Tassetto et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Integration of viral nucleic acids into the insect genome creates a long-lasting and heritable immune memory.
claims.source: In this system, endogenous transposons Ty1 and Ty3 play a central role in acquiring copies of viral nucleic acids and integrating them into the genome, thus creating a long-lasting and heritable immune memory (Saleh et al., 2009; Tassetto et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Saleh et al., 2009; Tassetto et al., 2017.

claims.claim: There are intriguing parallels in the convergent evolution of mechanisms of acquired immunity.
claims.source: These examples reveal intriguing parallels in the convergent evolution of mechanisms of acquired immunity (Eaglesham and Kranzusch, 2024), all of which exploit the enzymatic activities of genes acquired from domesticated retrotransposons to establish immune memory by modifying host genomic information.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Eaglesham and Kranzusch, 2024.

claims.claim: Insects are the most abundant group of animals on Earth.
claims.source: Insects are the most abundant group of animals on Earth (Stork, 2018), and like other animals, they are exposed to a wide range of pathogens throughout their lifetimes, including viruses, bacteria, fungi, protozoa, nematodes, and parasitoids (Federici, 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Stork, 2018.

claims.claim: Insects are exposed to a wide range of pathogens including viruses, bacteria, fungi, protozoa, nematodes, and parasitoids.
claims.source: Insects are the most abundant group of animals on Earth (Stork, 2018), and like other animals, they are exposed to a wide range of pathogens throughout their lifetimes, including viruses, bacteria, fungi, protozoa, nematodes, and parasitoids (Federici, 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Federici, 2009.

claims.claim: Insects can act as reservoirs for pathogens, serving as vectors that facilitate their amplification and transmission, including to humans.
claims.source: In such cases, insects can act as reservoirs for these pathogens, serving as vectors that facilitate their amplification and transmission, including to humans (St Leger, 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to St Leger, 2021.

claims.claim: The cuticle acts as a physical barrier in insects, offering strong protection against most pathogens in the environment.
claims.source: In insects, the primary immune defense is provided by the cuticle, which acts as a physical barrier, offering strong protection against most pathogens in the environment.
claims.evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The most common routes of infection in insects are through wounds, the digestive system, or the tracheal system.
claims.source: Consequently, the most common routes of infection are through wounds, the digestive system, or the tracheal system.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about insect infection routes.

claims.claim: Once the cuticle is breached, immune cells are activated, triggering both cellular and humoral immune responses.
claims.source: Once the cuticle is breached, immune cells are activated, triggering both cellular and humoral immune responses (Buchon et al., 2014; Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Buchon et al., 2014 and illustrated in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The insect innate immune system is largely based on evolutionarily conserved pathways that are also found in mammals.
claims.source: The insect innate immune system is largely based on evolutionarily conserved pathways, which are also found, to some extent, in mammals.
claims.evidence: This represents established knowledge in comparative immunology.

claims.claim: The cellular branch of insect immunity includes various effector immune cells known as hemocytes.
claims.source: The cellular branch includes various effector immune cells, known as hemocytes, which perform distinct functions during the immune response, such as phagocytosis (plasmatocytes), encapsulation (lamellocytes), activation of phenoloxidases (crystal cells), degranulation (granulocytes), or the release of extracellular traps (Mahanta et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Mahanta et al., 2023 and illustrated in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Plasmatocytes perform phagocytosis during the immune response.
claims.source: The cellular branch includes various effector immune cells, known as hemocytes, which perform distinct functions during the immune response, such as phagocytosis (plasmatocytes), encapsulation (lamellocytes), activation of phenoloxidases (crystal cells), degranulation (granulocytes), or the release of extracellular traps (Mahanta et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Mahanta et al., 2023 and illustrated in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Lamellocytes perform encapsulation during the immune response.
claims.source: The cellular branch includes various effector immune cells, known as hemocytes, which perform distinct functions during the immune response, such as phagocytosis (plasmatocytes), encapsulation (lamellocytes), activation of phenoloxidases (crystal cells), degranulation (granulocytes), or the release of extracellular traps (Mahanta et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Mahanta et al., 2023 and illustrated in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Crystal cells activate phenoloxidases during the immune response.
claims.source: The cellular branch includes various effector immune cells, known as hemocytes, which perform distinct functions during the immune response, such as phagocytosis (plasmatocytes), encapsulation (lamellocytes), activation of phenoloxidases (crystal cells), degranulation (granulocytes), or the release of extracellular traps (Mahanta et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Mahanta et al., 2023 and illustrated in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Some insect species possess specialized immune cell types including spherulocytes, oenocytoids, coagulocytes, adipohemocytes, and thrombocytoids.
claims.source: In addition, some insect species possess specialized immune cell types, such as spherulocytes, oenocytoids, coagulocytes, adipohemocytes, and thrombocytoids, which further contribute to pathogen elimination, wound healing, metabolic homeostasis, as well as nutrient transport (Eleftherianos et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Eleftherianos et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Extracellular traps are composed of double-stranded DNA, histones, elastase, and myeloperoxidase.
claims.source: These extracellular web-like structures, composed of double-stranded DNA, histones, elastase, and myeloperoxidase, serve to trap, immobilize, and kill pathogens (Nascimento et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Nascimento et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Key signaling pathways and transcription factors involved in phagocytosis, hematopoiesis, cell proliferation, and differentiation have remained conserved for over 550 million years of evolution.
claims.source: Although insect immune cell types and their functions are less diverse than those in vertebrates, the key signaling pathways and transcription factors involved in phagocytosis (Melcarne et al., 2019), hematopoiesis (Banerjee et al., 2019), cell proliferation, and differentiation (Evans et al., 2003) have remained conserved for over 550 million years of evolution.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Melcarne et al., 2019; Banerjee et al., 2019; Evans et al., 2003.

claims.claim: Pathogen recognition receptors can be classified into several groups including NOD-like receptors, C-type lectins, thioester-containing proteins, scavenger receptors, peptidoglycan recognition proteins, Toll-like receptors, and Gram-negative-binding proteins.
claims.source: Pathogens are detected by pathogen recognition receptors that can be classified into several groups, such as NOD-like receptors, C-type lectins, thioester-containing proteins, scavenger receptors, peptidoglycan recognition proteins, Toll-like receptors, or Gram-negative-binding proteins.
claims.evidence: This represents established knowledge about insect immune recognition.

claims.claim: Gram-positive bacteria and fungi predominately activate the Toll pathway.
claims.source: While Gram-positive bacteria and fungi predominately activate the Toll pathway, Gram-negative bacteria induce the IMD signaling pathway (Browne et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Browne et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Gram-negative bacteria induce the IMD signaling pathway.
claims.source: While Gram-positive bacteria and fungi predominately activate the Toll pathway, Gram-negative bacteria induce the IMD signaling pathway (Browne et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Browne et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Insects utilize encapsulation and melanization when encountering foreign objects too large for phagocytosis.
claims.source: When encountering foreign objects too large for phagocytosis, such as parasitoid eggs or nematodes, insects utilize encapsulation and melanization (Bilandžija et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Bilandžija et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Prophenoloxidases catalyze the conversion of phenylalanine and tyrosine into melanin, producing toxic free radical by-products.
claims.source: These enzymes catalyze the conversion of the amino acids phenylalanine and tyrosine into melanin, producing toxic free radical by-products that help eliminate the pathogen (Tang, 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Tang, 2009.

claims.claim: The conserved intracellular immune response based on RNA interference (RNAi) is the most thoroughly studied antiviral mechanism in insects.
claims.source: The conserved intracellular immune response based on RNA interference (RNAi) remains the most thoroughly studied antiviral mechanism in insects (Gammon and Mello, 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Gammon and Mello, 2015.

claims.claim: Viral double-stranded RNA is cleaved by the endoribonuclease Dicer into short small interfering RNA (siRNA) fragments.
claims.source: In this pathway, viral double-stranded RNA is cleaved by the endoribonuclease Dicer into short small interfering RNA (siRNA) fragments.
claims.evidence: This describes the established RNAi mechanism.

claims.claim: Dicer and Argonaut form the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC), which facilitates sequence-specific recognition and cleavage of viral nucleic acids.
claims.source: Dicer, together with the RNA-dependent nuclease Argonaut, forms the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC), which facilitates the sequence-specific recognition and cleavage of viral nucleic acids (Leggewie and Schnettler, 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Leggewie and Schnettler, 2018.

claims.claim: The cGAS-like receptor STING-Relish pathway plays a central role in general antiviral defense in Drosophila.
claims.source: While the interferon response characteristic of mammalian species has not been identified in insects, recent findings suggest that the cGAS-like receptor STING-Relish pathway plays a central role in general antiviral defense in Drosophila.
claims.evidence: This is based on recent findings in the field.

claims.claim: STING signaling activates the IMD pathway transcription factor Relish to regulate the expression of genes potentially involved in antiviral defense.
claims.source: Similarly, in insects, it has been documented that STING signaling activates the IMD pathway transcription factor Relish to regulate the expression of genes potentially involved in antiviral defense (Goto et al., 2018; Decout et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Goto et al., 2018; Decout et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Insect plasmatocytes undergo metabolic rewiring in response to acute bacterial infection, shifting from oxidative phosphorylation to aerobic glycolysis.
claims.source: Similar to mammalian macrophages, insect plasmatocytes undergo a fundamental metabolic rewiring in response to acute bacterial infection, shifting their predominant ATP metabolic pathway from oxidative phosphorylation to aerobic glycolysis (Krejčová et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Krejčová et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Plasmatocytes secrete Imaginal morphogenesis protein late 2 to induce nutrient mobilization from the central metabolic organ.
claims.source: To secure these resources, plasmatocytes secrete various factors, such as Imaginal morphogenesis protein late 2, to induce nutrient mobilization from the central metabolic organ while limiting their consumption by peripheral nonimmune tissues.
claims.evidence: This is based on research findings described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Antimicrobial peptides are rapidly expressed by immune cells and the fat body during systemic infection.
claims.source: During systemic infection, antimicrobial peptides are rapidly expressed by immune cells and the fat body (Zhang et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Antimicrobial peptides act as opsonizing factors, embedding themselves in the hydrophobic portion of bacterial or fungal membrane.
claims.source: Due to their positive charge, these peptides act as opsonizing factors, embedding themselves in the hydrophobic portion of bacterial or fungal membrane. This facilitates recognition by immune cells, destabilizes the pathogen's membrane, and ultimately leads to cell death (Dho et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Dho et al., 2023.

claims.claim: Clotting proteins are cross-linked by transglutaminase, which is homologous to factor XIIIa in vertebrates.
claims.source: These molecules are cross-linked by transglutaminase, which is homologous to factor XIIIa, a key component of the vertebrate coagulation cascade.
claims.evidence: This represents established knowledge about insect clotting mechanisms.

claims.claim: The ability of the insect immune system to develop acquired immunity has been documented in a wide range of species.
claims.source: The ability of the insect immune system to develop some form of acquired immunity has been documented in a wide range of species (Cooper and Eleftherianos, 2017; Kurtz and Franz, 2003; Trauer-Kizilelma and Hilker, 2015; Freitak et al., 2009; Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Flies inoculated with an avirulent strain of Pseudomonas aeruginosa mount increased resistance to a highly virulent strain.
claims.source: In this study, the authors demonstrated that flies that were first inoculated with an avirulent strain of Pseudomonas aeruginosa mount an increased resistance to a highly virulent strain.
claims.evidence: This describes experimental findings from a cited study.

claims.claim: Flies primed with either a sublethal dose or heat-killed Streptococcus pneumoniae were protected against a lethal challenge of the same bacterium administered 7 days later.
claims.source: Flies primed with either a sublethal dose or heat-killed Streptococcus pneumoniae were protected against a lethal challenge of the same bacterium administered 7 days later, allowing sufficient time for pathogen clearance.
claims.evidence: This describes experimental findings from Pham et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Administration of a sublethal dose of Beauveria bassiana provided protection against a subsequent lethal dose of the same fungus.
claims.source: A similar effect was achieved by administering a sublethal dose of the natural fungal pathogen Beauveria bassiana, which provided protection against a subsequent lethal dose of the same fungus.
claims.evidence: This describes experimental findings from Pham et al., 2007.

claims.claim: A remarkably high degree of specificity of immune memory has been documented in Tribolium castaneum, whose immune system can discriminate between closely related bacterial strains of Bacillus thuringiensis.
claims.source: A remarkably high degree of specificity of immune memory has been documented in Tribolium castaneum, whose immune system can discriminate between closely related bacterial strains of Bacillus thuringiensis (Roth et al., 2009; Futo et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Roth et al., 2009; Futo et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Immune memory in bumblebees lasts for several weeks after clearance of bacteria from the first exposure.
claims.source: Narrow specificity and increased protection have also been observed in the bumblebee, Bombus terrestris, where the immune memory lasts for several weeks after clearance of bacteria from the first exposure (Sadd and Schmid-Hempel, 2006).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Sadd and Schmid-Hempel, 2006.

claims.claim: Adult flies orally infected with Drosophila C virus during the larval stage exhibited increased tolerance to subsequent reinfections with the same virus.
claims.source: Mondotte and colleagues conducted trans-stadial assays, revealing that adult flies orally infected with Drosophila C virus during the larval stage exhibited increased tolerance to subsequent reinfections with the same virus.
claims.evidence: This describes experimental findings from Mondotte et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Trans-stadial acquired immunity has been documented in Aedes aegypti, where infection of larvae with inactive dengue virus protects against subsequent infection in adult mosquitoes.
claims.source: Trans-stadial acquired immunity has also been documented in Aedes aegypti, where infection of larvae with inactive dengue virus has been shown to protect against subsequent infection in adult mosquitoes (Vargas et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Vargas et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Larval exposure to Streptococcus pyogenes or E. coli led to increased longevity of adult Anopheles arabiensis females challenged with the respective pathogen.
claims.source: Trans-stadial protection has also been documented in another mosquito, Anopheles arabiensis. In this study, larval exposure to Streptococcus pyogenes or E. coli led to increased longevity of adult females challenged with the respective pathogen (Patel and Oliver, 2024).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Patel and Oliver, 2024.

claims.claim: Adult Tribolium confusum beetles infested with Gregarina minuta display enhanced survival resistance when infected as larvae.
claims.source: Indeed, this model has shown that adult beetles infested with G. minuta display enhanced survival resistance when infected as larvae, highlighting the persistence of immune protection across life stages (Thomas and Rudolf, 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Thomas and Rudolf, 2010.

claims.claim: Transgenerational immune priming is likely to evolve in environments where offspring have a high probability of encountering the same pathogen as their parents.
claims.source: Since mounting an immune response is connected with significant energy costs, TgIP is likely to evolve in environments where offspring have a high probability of encountering the same pathogen as their parents (Thomas and Rudolf, 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Thomas and Rudolf, 2010.

claims.claim: Larvae of immunized honeybee queens display improved survival compared to larval progeny of nonimmunized queens when fed Paenibacillus larvae spores.
claims.source: It has been shown that these individuals display improved survival compared to larval progeny of nonimmunized queens. This enhanced survival was presumably due to a threefold increase in the number of differential hemocytes (all hemocyte types except for prohemocytes) (Hernández López et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Hernández López et al., 2014.

claims.claim: When bumblebee queens were challenged with heat-killed Arthrobacter globiformis, both their eggs and progeny workers exhibited significantly higher antibacterial activity when injected by lipopolysaccharides.
claims.source: When queens were challenged with heat-killed Arthrobacter globiformis, both their eggs and progeny workers exhibited significantly higher antibacterial activity when injected by lipopolysaccharides, compared to controls (Sadd and Schmid-Hempel, 2007).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Sadd and Schmid-Hempel, 2007.

claims.claim: Transgenerational immune priming has been connected with certain costs, as individuals were more susceptible to a pathogen distinct from maternal challenge.
claims.source: However, such TgIP has been connected with certain costs since these individuals were more susceptible to a pathogen distinct from maternal challenge, the trypanosome parasite Crithidia bombi (Sadd and Schmid-Hempel, 2007).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Sadd and Schmid-Hempel, 2007.

claims.claim: Female offspring of immunized Manduca sexta parents laid fewer eggs than those derived from control parents.
claims.source: The costs of TgIP have also been investigated in tobacco hornworm Manduca sexta, where female offspring of immunized parents laid fewer eggs than those derived from control parents (Trauer and Hilker, 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Trauer and Hilker, 2013.

claims.claim: After parental exposure to heat-killed E. coli or B. thuringiensis, transgenerational immune priming occurs through fathers as well as mothers in Tribolium castaneum.
claims.source: After parental exposure to heat-killed E. coli or B. thuringiensis, TgIP occurs through fathers as well as mothers (Roth et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Roth et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Offspring of Indian meal moth parents exposed to a low dose of their natural DNA virus during the larval stage were less susceptible to viral challenge.
claims.source: Offspring of Indian meal moth (Plodia interpunctella) parents exposed to a low dose of their natural DNA virus during the larval stage were less susceptible to viral challenge (Tidbury et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Tidbury et al., 2011.

claims.claim: The offspring of immune-challenged parents inherit viral DNA and exhibit upregulation of genes related to chromatin and DNA binding.
claims.source: Using D. melanogaster and A. aegypti as models, the authors revealed that the offspring of immune-challenged parents inherit viral DNA and exhibit upregulation of genes related to chromatin and DNA binding (Mondotte et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Mondotte et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Aedes aegypti mosquitoes infected with arboviruses can transmit specific immunity to their offspring.
claims.source: Similar results were obtained in a recent study by Rodriguez-Andres and colleagues, who documented that A. aegypti mosquitoes infected with arboviruses can transmit specific immunity to their offspring (Rodriguez-Andres et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Rodriguez-Andres et al., 2024.

claims.claim: Alterations in the epigenetic landscape, specifically DNA methylation and histone acetylation, were detected in the F1 generation of parents fed non-pathogenic E. coli or Serratia entomophila.
claims.source: Additionally, alterations in the epigenetic landscape, specifically DNA methylation and histone acetylation, were detected in the F1 generation of parents fed non-pathogenic E. coli or the entomopathogen Serratia entomophila (Gegner et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Gegner et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Immune memory appears to persist through developmental stages and may be passed on to subsequent generations in insects.
claims.source: Moreover, immune memory appears to persist through developmental stages and may even be passed on to subsequent generations.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the evidence presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Acquired immune memory can be divided into three phases: antigen acquisition, development of immune specificity, and maintenance of immune memory.
claims.source: Acquired immune memory can be in general divided into three phases
claims.evidence: This is a conceptual framework presented by the authors.

claims.claim: Virus-infected cells activate the transcription factors Hop and Dome, leading to increased production of unpaired family cytokines.
claims.source: Virus-infected cells commonly activate the transcription factors Hop and Dome, leading to increased production of unpaired family cytokines (Upd1, Upd2, Upd3).
claims.evidence: This describes established mechanisms of insect antiviral immunity.

claims.claim: Elevated levels of unpaired cytokines in circulation activate macrophage-like plasmatocytes via the JAK-STAT signaling pathway.
claims.source: Elevated levels of these cytokines in circulation activate macrophage-like plasmatocytes via the JAK-STAT signaling pathway, attracting them to virus-infected tissues (Sabin et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Sabin et al., 2010.

claims.claim: The elimination of virus-infected apoptotic cells by activated plasmatocytes is crucial for viral resistance in Drosophila.
claims.source: The elimination of virus-infected apoptotic cells by activated plasmatocytes has been shown to be crucial for viral resistance in Drosophila (Saleh et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Saleh et al., 2009.

claims.claim: The presence of viral double-stranded RNA in the phagolysosome leads to permeabilization of its membrane and acquisition of viral genetic information.
claims.source: However, plasmatocytes do not simply degrade all engulfed material; the presence of viral double-stranded RNA in the phagolysosome leads to permeabilization of its membrane and acquisition of viral genetic information (Tanaka et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Tanaka et al., 2024.

claims.claim: Plasmatocytes use viral RNA as a template for reverse transcription, integrating fragments of complementary antisense viral DNA into their genomes.
claims.source: Plasmatocytes then use viral RNA as a template for reverse transcription, integrating fragments of complementary antisense viral DNA into their genomes (Tassetto et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Tassetto et al., 2017 and illustrated in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Retrotransposon activity increases more than 20-fold in plasmatocytes upon viral infection.
claims.source: Nevertheless, retrotransposon activity increases more than 20-fold in plasmatocytes upon viral infection, and mere inhibition of retrotransposons completely abolishes the host's resistance to infection.
claims.evidence: This describes experimental findings on retrotransposon activity.

results.result: Insects can develop long-term, pathogen-specific immune memory that can be transmitted to offspring, challenging the traditional view that insects rely solely on innate immunity. However, the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 establish the central premise of the review: that experimental evidence has overturned the traditional view of insect immunity (C1-C2), including transgenerational transmission (C3), while acknowledging gaps in mechanistic understanding (C4). These claims are well-supported by extensive experimental evidence cited throughout the manuscript and form the foundation for the review's focus.

results.result: Three categories of acquired immune responses are distinguished based on temporal dynamics and specificity: immune priming (persistent activation), immune training (biphasic, non-specific), and immune memory (biphasic, pathogen-specific).
results.evaluation: Claims C9 and C13-C16 define the conceptual framework for categorizing acquired immunity, supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1. The distinctions between persistent vs. biphasic responses and specific vs. non-specific immunity provide clear criteria for classification, though the manuscript acknowledges that experimental designs don't always allow clear distinction between these categories.

results.result: More than 150 prokaryotic immune mechanisms have been identified, many of which are conserved in eukaryotes, suggesting that immune mechanisms evolved in prokaryotes were later adopted by eukaryotic immune systems, likely through horizontal gene transfer mediated by retrotransposons.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C21 present a well-supported evolutionary framework based on comparative genomics (C17-C19) and cite the prevailing hypothesis for mechanism transfer (C20-C21). The evidence from whole-genome sequencing and the identification of conserved mechanisms across the tree of life provides strong support, though C20-C21 are explicitly presented as hypotheses rather than proven mechanisms.

results.result: The CRISPR-Cas system in prokaryotes serves as adaptive immunity by integrating viral DNA fragments into the host genome (CRISPR locus), which upon subsequent infection produces CRISPR RNAs that guide Cas nucleases to perform sequence-specific cleavage of viral genetic material.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C28 describe the well-established CRISPR-Cas mechanism, supported by multiple citations to established literature. This serves as a comparative framework for understanding insect immune memory mechanisms discussed later in the manuscript. The mechanism is presented as established knowledge rather than novel findings.

results.result: Key immune enzymes across diverse organisms, including prokaryotic defense enzymes, vertebrate Rag1/Rag2, and insect antiviral proteins, are derived from domesticated retrotransposons, revealing convergent evolution in acquired immunity mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C33 establish a pattern of convergent evolution supported by citations. The evidence spans prokaryotes (C29), vertebrates (C30), and insects (C31-C32), with C33 synthesizing these examples into a broader evolutionary principle. The claims are well-supported by cited literature, though C31-C32 reference mechanisms discussed in detail later in the manuscript.

results.result: The insect immune system consists of physical barriers (cuticle), cellular immunity (diverse hemocyte types performing phagocytosis, encapsulation, and other functions), and is based on evolutionarily conserved pathways found in mammals, with key signaling components conserved for over 550 million years.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C47 provide a comprehensive overview of insect immunity, supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 2. The description of physical barriers, cellular components, and evolutionary conservation is well-established in the literature. These claims provide essential background for understanding how acquired immunity could function within this system.

results.result: Insect pathogen recognition involves multiple receptor classes that activate specific signaling pathways (Toll for Gram-positive bacteria/fungi, IMD for Gram-negative bacteria), with responses including encapsulation/melanization for large pathogens and RNAi-based antiviral defense involving Dicer and RISC complex.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C55 describe established mechanisms of insect pathogen recognition and response, supported by citations. The specificity of pathway activation (C49-C50) and the description of RNAi mechanisms (C53-C55) are well-documented in the literature and provide context for understanding how specificity could arise in immune memory.

results.result: Insect antiviral defense involves the STING-Relish pathway, metabolic rewiring of plasmatocytes from oxidative phosphorylation to aerobic glycolysis, and humoral factors including antimicrobial peptides and clotting proteins with homology to vertebrate coagulation factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C62 describe recent findings (C56-C57) and established mechanisms (C58-C62) of insect immune responses, all supported by citations. The metabolic rewiring (C58-C59) and humoral responses (C60-C62) demonstrate the complexity and conservation of insect immunity, providing context for understanding immune memory maintenance.

results.result: Acquired immunity has been documented across diverse insect species, with experiments in Drosophila, Tribolium castaneum, and Bombus terrestris demonstrating pathogen-specific protection lasting days to weeks after pathogen clearance, including discrimination between closely related bacterial strains.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C68 present experimental evidence for acquired immunity across multiple species, supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 3. The specificity demonstrated in T. castaneum (C67) and duration in B. terrestris (C68) are particularly strong evidence for true immune memory rather than priming. However, the manuscript notes that some early Drosophila studies (C64) may represent priming rather than memory due to short intervals between exposures.

results.result: Trans-stadial immune memory has been documented in multiple insect species, where larval pathogen exposure provides protection in adults, including virus-specific protection in Drosophila and mosquitoes, and bacterial protection in Anopheles and Tribolium.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C72 demonstrate that immune memory can persist through metamorphosis, supported by citations to experimental studies. The virus-specific protection in Drosophila (C69) is particularly compelling as it demonstrates specificity. The persistence across complete metamorphosis suggests stable memory mechanisms, though the underlying molecular basis is not fully explained.

results.result: Transgenerational immune priming (TgIP) has been documented in multiple insect species, where parental pathogen exposure enhances offspring immunity through both maternal and paternal routes, with evidence of viral DNA inheritance, epigenetic modifications, and associated fitness costs.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C82 present extensive evidence for TgIP across diverse species (honeybees, bumblebees, beetles, moths, flies, mosquitoes), supported by multiple citations. The demonstration of both maternal and paternal transmission (C78), viral DNA inheritance (C80-C81), and epigenetic changes (C82) provides mechanistic insights. The documented costs (C76-C77) add credibility by showing trade-offs. This represents a major finding challenging traditional views of inheritance.

results.result: Insect antiviral immune memory involves three phases: (1) plasmatocytes eliminate virus-infected cells and acquire viral RNA from phagolysosomes, (2) viral RNA is reverse transcribed and integrated into the genome via retrotransposon activity (>20-fold increase), creating endogenous viral elements (EVEs), and (3) EVEs produce secondary viral DNAs that prime RNAi machinery and are disseminated systemically via extracellular vesicles.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C95 present a detailed mechanistic model supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 4. The evidence includes the role of plasmatocytes (C85-C87), phagolysosome permeabilization (C88), reverse transcription (C89), retrotransposon involvement (C90-C91), EVE formation (C92), and systemic dissemination (C94-C95). The >20-fold increase in retrotransposon activity (C90) and the requirement for retrotransposons provide strong mechanistic support. This represents the most complete mechanistic understanding in the manuscript.

results.result: Insect antiviral immune memory, based on genomic integration of viral sequences for sequence-specific elimination, is analogous to CRISPR-Cas systems, provides transgenerational immunity, and appears widespread across arthropods (insects, ticks, crustaceans), with some species utilizing both siRNA and piRNA pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C101 synthesize the antiviral mechanism and its distribution, supported by citations. The CRISPR analogy (C96) is appropriate given the shared principle of genomic integration. The evidence for widespread distribution (C98-C99) is based on comparative analysis of small RNAs from EVE regions, though this is inferential rather than direct experimental demonstration in all species. The piRNA pathway variation (C100-C101) adds mechanistic diversity.

results.result: Evidence suggests that RNAi-based antiviral immunity may exist in mammals, with virus-derived siRNAs spreading systemically via extracellular vesicles, though contradictory findings indicate Dicer has negligible activity in virus-infected mammalian cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103 present conflicting evidence about RNAi in mammalian antiviral immunity. While C102 provides evidence for siRNA spread and acquired resistance, C103 presents contradictory findings about Dicer activity. The manuscript appropriately presents this as uncertain and requiring further investigation. The evidence is insufficient to conclude whether a CRISPR-like mechanism exists in mammals.

results.result: Although insects lack MHC and tapasin genes, heterologous expression of these genes in Drosophila S2 cells enables antigen presentation, suggesting conserved antigen processing machinery. Mammalian macrophages disseminate antigens via extracellular vesicles and eruptophagy, and bacterial antigens are found complexed with hemolymph proteins in insects.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C107 address the critical question of antigen acquisition in insects. The S2 cell experiment (C105) demonstrates that the machinery for antigen presentation exists even without MHC/tapasin. The evidence for antigen dissemination in mammals (C106) and antigen-protein complexes in insects (C107) suggests possible mechanisms, though direct evidence for how antigens are processed and distributed in insects remains limited. This represents an important gap in understanding antibacterial immune memory.

results.result: Dscam, consisting of extracellular immunoglobulin domains, transmembrane region, and cytosolic tail, can generate up to 19,008 variants through mutually exclusive alternative splicing of three multivariant exons (12×48×33 combinations), making it the gene with the highest number of alternative transcripts in animals, with splicing regulated by docking/selector sequences and >12 RNA-binding proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C116 describe the structure and diversity of Dscam, supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 5. The calculation of 19,008 variants (C112) is mathematically correct based on the exon variants. The complexity of splicing regulation (C114-C115) is well-documented. This establishes Dscam as having sufficient diversity to potentially recognize diverse pathogens, analogous to antibody diversity in vertebrates.

results.result: Dscam plays a dual role in insects: in CNS development, where combinations of splicing variants provide each neuron with a unique recognition code, and homodimeric DSCAM interactions trigger cytoskeletal remodeling and cellular repulsion to prevent self-stimulating loops.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C120 describe the well-established role of Dscam in neural development, supported by citations. This provides important context for understanding Dscam function and establishes the principle of homodimeric recognition (C119-C120), which is proposed to function similarly in immune responses. The neural function is presented as established knowledge rather than novel findings.

results.result: During bacterial infection, Dscam is highly expressed in plasmatocytes, producing both circulating and membrane-bound DSCAM forms that facilitate pathogen opsonization and phagocytosis. Alternative splicing produces nearly the full DSCAM repertoire, but infection by specific pathogens results in selection of specific Dscam variants with high affinity for pathogen surface antigens.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C126 describe Dscam's role in immunity, supported by citations. The key finding is pathogen-specific selection of Dscam variants (C126), which provides a mechanism for specificity analogous to antibody selection. However, C123 notes that the mechanism of recognition is believed rather than proven, and questions remain about whether homodimeric binding is required. The evidence supports a role in immunity but mechanistic details remain incomplete.

results.result: In crustaceans, DSCAM binding to pathogens triggers internalization via homodimeric interaction, activating Dock and downstream kinases (MAPK-ERK-JNK), leading to antimicrobial peptide production and altered hnRNP/SR-protein ratios that may stabilize alternative splicing. DSCAM is then cleaved by ADAM and γ-secretase, with the cytosolic domain translocating to the nucleus to promote cell persistence and proliferation.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C133 present a detailed signaling model primarily from crustacean studies, supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 6. The signaling cascade (C128-C130) is well-documented, though the mechanism by which altered hnRNP/SR ratios stabilize specific splicing (C131) is presented as speculative ('may'). The nuclear translocation and proliferation program (C133) provides a potential mechanism for memory maintenance. However, the manuscript notes that direct evidence in insects is limited.

results.result: While infection-induced proliferation is common in larval/pupal insects, some adult insects with documented immune memory show limited proliferative potential and lack identified hematopoietic organs for memory maintenance. Dscam mRNA might be stored in membraneless organelles like p-bodies or ω-speckles.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C136 highlight a critical gap in understanding memory maintenance. While C134 documents proliferation in some life stages, C135 notes its absence in adults of some species with documented memory, creating a paradox. The speculation about mRNA storage (C136) is presented as a hypothesis without direct experimental support. This represents an important unresolved question requiring future research.

results.result: Drosophila offers unparalleled genetic tools (Gal4-UAS system) for tissue-specific gene manipulation, and the insect immune system shows evolutionarily conserved features with mammalian innate immunity. Since insects evolved over 400 million years ago, their ability to remember infections without adaptive immunity suggests innate immune memory is a fundamental trait predating vertebrate adaptive immunity.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C138 describe established capabilities of Drosophila as a model system, supported by citations. Claims C139-C141 present the evolutionary argument for studying insect immunity, with C140 stating established knowledge and C141 drawing an inference about the fundamental nature of innate immune memory. The inference is logical but represents interpretation rather than direct evidence. The claims effectively argue for the value of Drosophila research.

results.result: Innate immune memory formation involves epigenetic modifications (DNA methylation, histone acetylation) that persist after infection clearance, and can be transmitted to offspring, enabling challenged parents to produce progeny with enhanced immune defenses. Vaccination represents one of the most significant breakthroughs in immunology.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C143 summarize evidence for epigenetic mechanisms in immune memory and transgenerational transmission, supported by citation to Gegner et al., 2019 and evidence presented earlier (C82). Claim C144 provides context for the potential applications. These claims synthesize earlier findings and set up the discussion of insect vaccination potential.

results.result: Preliminary experiments demonstrate that injection or feeding of viral nucleic acids alone, bacterial components (LPS), or attenuated pathogens can provide acquired immunity in insects, with protective effects observed in mosquitoes (as few as 10^5 viral RNA copies), beetles, and honeybees against viruses, fungi, and bacteria.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C149 present experimental evidence for insect vaccination approaches, all supported by citations. The diversity of approaches (nucleic acids, LPS, attenuated pathogens) and target organisms (mosquitoes, beetles, honeybees) demonstrates feasibility. The quantification in mosquitoes (C146) provides practical parameters. The successful treatment of American foulbrood (C149) demonstrates real-world application. This represents promising applied research building on mechanistic understanding.

results.result: Honeybee colonies face threats from viral and bacterial diseases, while blood-feeding insects transmit diseases claiming millions of victims annually. These vectors show high tolerance to pathogens, making them ideal reservoirs. Manipulating vector immune tolerance is a considered strategy to reduce pathogen spread and disease incidence.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C153 establish the applied significance of insect immune memory research, supported by citations. The identification of two major problems (pollinator health and vector-borne disease) provides clear motivation for the research. Claim C153 presents immune manipulation as a strategy under consideration, appropriately citing Lambrechts and Saleh, 2019. These claims effectively argue for the practical importance of understanding insect immune memory.
